claims.text: The starting material is a compositionally complex, single-phase HEA with a homogeneous microstructure and no detectable coarse precipitates or second phases.
Brittle behavior in initially single-phase HEAs can emerge from localized chemical ordering associated with minor-element segregation at grain boundaries.
Minor-element segregation at grain boundaries reduces intergranular cohesion under service loading.
The proposed brittle behavior occurs without gross intermetallic precipitation.
Coarse precipitates and phase separation are the dominant causes of embrittlement in conventional alloys.
Controlled thermal aging or deformation increases atomic mobility and permits minor elements to segregate to grain boundaries.
A treatment regime can promote grain-boundary segregation without triggering bulk phase separation.
Moderately high service temperatures amplify grain-boundary segregation kinetics while the alloy remains single phase.
Thermally activated diffusion promotes migration and local enrichment of selected alloying elements at grain boundaries.
Mechanical stress promotes migration and local enrichment of selected alloying elements at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary enrichment weakens local atomic bonding and grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes a drop in toughness and a transition toward brittle failure despite the absence of brittle precipitates.
Relative to the untreated state, treated material will have lower fracture energy.
Relative to the untreated state, treated material will have lower ductility.
Relative to the untreated state, treated material will show more intergranular fracture features.
The untreated HEA has high ductility and toughness under the same test conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies only where temperature permits atomic mobility but does not cause phase separation or rapid grain growth.
The proposed mechanism applies under loading conditions that stress grain boundaries without catastrophic damage from competing mechanisms.
The critical segregating minor elements and the quantitative segregation kinetics are unknown.

A treated-versus-untreated comparison combining grain-boundary characterization, toughness testing, tensile testing, and fractography can test the proposed association between segregation and embrittlement.
